title: Hulu’s Rumored Clavicular Doc Is Actually a True Crime Series (Exclusive)
full_text: Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All October 26, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source A still from 'Get Huge,' a Hulu documentary on Looksmaxxing Hulu/Disney Logo text Look(smaxx) here: We finally have actual information on that rumored Clavicular Hulu documentary. The Hollywood Reporter can first reveal that all that beef between the 20-year-old looksmaxxer, whose real name is Braden Peters, and Disney has resulted in a three-part true crime documentary series titled Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death . The Hulu doc is not and was never a documentary about Peters, rather it was about the dangerous and competitive worlds of looksmaxxing and social media; Peters just happens to be the most famous individual on that scene and his likeness is only used briefly. Specifically, the docuseries is about a mysterious death in Thailand (that has nothing whatsoever to do with Clavicular). But since it’s been a while, the backstory: Peters served Disney/Hulu a cease and desist letter after he says he caught documentarians Jennings Brown and James Kristofik filming him backstage at the Elena Velez fashion show in February New York City without permission. Peters did not like that, but the encounter would be far from his biggest legal case this year. Just last week, Peters pleaded not guilty to raping an underage girl after she was given alcohol while appearing on his livestream in 2025. In September, Peters was charged with two felony counts, one for rape and another for drugging a person for sexual intercourse. He also faces a misdemeanor count for providing alcohol to someone younger than 21. Peters has denied the allegations, saying that the encounter was consensual. He has posted a video to his social media accounts showing screenshots of a text conversation and a photo of a handwritten letter, which were intercut over footage of Peters, shirtless and fixing his hair at an urban inner harbor. Beneath the posts, he’s written, “Theres better ways to make money then suing someone because they don’t want you,” and “Yeah still texting me to this day… totally not just trying to be greedy and get a check.” Braden “Clavicular” Peters walks the runway during New York Fashion Week earlier this year. Victor VIRGILE/Gamma-Rapho/Getty Images Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death presents what producers call “an unflinching portrait of masculinity in the influencer age, where extreme biohacking, online performance and a series of suspicious deaths converge.” The series debuts Nov. 10 on Hulu (and Hulu on Disney+ for bundle subscribers) in the U.S. It will stream on Disney+ internationally. “Deep in the manosphere, an underground movement promises to unlock human potential — bulging muscles, bigger penises, eternal youth. At its center is Dr. Tony Huge, a guru pushing homemade biohacks on a devoted following willing to risk everything for the cause,” the logline reads. “When Leo & Longevity, a penis-enlargement expert and one of Tony’s closest allies, is found dead in Thailand, alpha-male influencers become online sleuths, running wild with theories and questioning Tony Huge and his right-hand man, Connor Murphy. Soon, a darker pattern emerges: Leo isn’t the first of the inner circle to die under mysterious circumstances. Will he be the last?” Get Huge: Looksmaxxing to Death is directed by Stacey Lee, and produced by Boardwalk Pictures ( Welcome to Wrexham , aka Charlie Sheen ) and Hyperobject Industries ( Don’t Look Up , Stormbound ). Executive producers include Adam McKay and Todd Schulman for Hyperobject Industries, Andrew Fried, Lana Barkin, Jordan Wynn and Dane Lillegard for Boardwalk Pictures, William Crouse and Stacey Lee for Lovely Days, Jennings Brown for Nocturne Media, and Brett Neichin. title: Zooey Deschanel on Holiday Plans, ‘New Girl’ Cast Hangs and Bath & Body Works Campaign
full_text: × Skip to main content By Chris Gardner Plus Icon Chris Gardner chrissgardner Follow Sign Up View All October 26, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Zooey Deschanel for Bath & Body Works' new holiday 2026 campaign. Courtesy of Bath & Body Works If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, The Hollywood Reporter may receive an affiliate commission. The holidays arrived early for Zooey Deschanel — and she’s loving every second. “I like to get into the Christmas or holiday season as soon as possible,” the veteran star explained to The Hollywood Reporter while seated inside a palatial mansion that had been turned into a veritable winter wonderland courtesy of Bath & Body Works on Oct. 21. The popular retailer recruited Deschanel to front its new Season of Wonder campaign that debuted today , so they hosted her along with press, VIPs and influencers at a Beverly Hills home that had been decorated with its fragrant offerings, Christmas trees, snow globes and plenty of pastel accoutrements to match the new collection. Related Stories TV Jake Johnson Teases New Project With 'New Girl' Co-Star Damon Wayans Jr. TV 'New Girl' Stars Reunite -- in a Slightly Different Way Than Max Greenfield Claimed The actress, fresh from wrapping the She & Him Tour with her bandmates and reuniting with her New Girl family at a fundraiser in L.A., opened up to THR about her favorite holiday traditions, the changing landscape of Hollywood for actors and performers and what she’s really itching to do on the work front. Why did you say yes to this partnership with Bath & Body Works? I feel very nostalgic about Bath & Body Works. It’s something I’ve loved since high school, and still love. It’s one of those things that just feels like a classic. I was also excited because I love the holidays, and Bath & Body Works has all these beautiful seasonal scents . It’s fun to experience the holidays fully every day, and having a different scent for every day makes that easy. What does it mean to experience the holidays fully? I want to feel like, “I did it. I did Christmas.” I want to be tired of Christmas by the time it ends — or after New Year’s — and think, “OK, I can be without this amazing, wonderful thing for 10 months now.” I love that you can live out the holidays fully through all the scents. If you’re not baking Christmas cookies or singing Christmas carols every day, you can experience the holidays in whatever way works for you. Everyone is different. Some people want to wear perfume every day, while others just want a subtle body wash. Some people like to light a candle; I love the home fragrance. I also love it for gifting because I enjoy giving gifts and picking out something special for my friends. Candles are a great gift because everyone is on a diet or not drinking now. People are trying to be so good. A candle is something you can enjoy even if you’re on a diet or not drinking alcohol. It’s almost the new etiquette of gift-giving in Hollywood. It’s gluten-free. ( Laughs .) Deschanel as “Holiday Wonder Maker” for Bath & Body Works’ new holiday 2026 campaign. Season of Wonder products are available now online and at Bath & Body Works stores with select products also available in Ulta stores, ulta.com and on Amazon . Courtesy of Bath & Body Works Do you have a favorite scent? What I love is that there are so many different ones to choose from, and you can express a different part of your personality every day. My favorite is Moonlit Goddess . I make them give me more of it because I love it so much. They make all of these scents in different forms, so you can enjoy them in pretty much any way you like. It’s a seasonal scent, but it feels very year-round to me. It smells like pears and lavender. [She uncovers a candle and offers it up to smell.] That’s good. It’s so smooth. It’s smooth. Are you someone who starts decorating for the holidays the day after Thanksgiving? The day after Halloween — if I can. It depends, but I like to get into the Christmas or holiday season as soon as possible. What are some other Zooey Deschanel holiday traditions you look forward to each year? I love making a huge batch of sugar cookies and letting my kids decorate them. Everything gets everywhere, but it’s so fun. They’re so proud of the cookies, and we put them out on Christmas and say, “We made these.” I love singing Christmas carols. I grew up in choirs, so singing Christmas carols feels very nostalgic for me. I love singing harmonies and singing with other people. I also love picking out gifts for people, thinking about their personalities and trying to give them something they’ll love. I love spending time with family, decorating for Christmas and coming up with themes. It’s all so fun. The holiday campaign marks the brand’s largest media buy to date with ads set to be splashed across YouTube, connected TV, social media, in-store and out-of-home placements in major markets like New York, Los Angeles and Dallas. Courtesy of Bath & Body Works Speaking of harmonies, congratulations on just finishing your She & Him Tour. How was it? It was so fun. We had a song go viral this year. It was something I wrote 25 years ago that was on our first record, and it ended up charting. It was nice to get to play it for a new group of people who maybe didn’t know our music before. There were lots and lots of young people. It was so much fun, and playing music is always such a joy for me. It was very exciting to get to do that. Did the tour feel different this time around? It was actually smaller than what we’ve done in the past. We used to tour with a lot more people, but this time we toured with fewer musicians. It was really fun to rearrange everything. We were doing mostly the material I wrote for our Volume One, Volume Two and Volume 3 records. That was really fun because we had been doing a lot of holiday tours. We have a couple of holiday records that we’re very proud of, and our last tour was, I think, a holiday tour. It was great to get back out there and play the songs from those records, then reimagine them with a smaller group. Everything sounded great. It was so much fun. View this post on Instagram You’ve also been busy with acting. Congratulations on the film Trash Mountain with Caleb Hearon, which premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival. Has it found a home yet? I think they’re very close to figuring that out, but I don’t have a final update. I’ll let you know once I know. We don’t want to get you in trouble. I don’t want to get in trouble. But I love that movie, and I’m so proud of it. We were all there because we loved the story, loved the script and loved Caleb. It’s a movie I’m immensely proud of, so I’m excited that people are seeing it and responding to it. Even if you hadn’t reunited with your New Girl friends recently, I feel like I’m still contractually obligated to ask you about New Girl. It’s in your contract. ( Laughs .) The New Girl reunion at the Chrysalis fundraiser went viral because seeing the cast back together warms so many hearts. Since you’re all still close and everyone likes each other, are we any closer to an official screen reunion of some sort? I don’t know because there’s a lot of legal stuff involved. There are many different entities and people involved. I wish I were the authority on that, but I’m very much not. I’m really close with everybody, though. That event was incredible, and hats off to Max [Greenfield] for getting everyone together. He worked so hard to make sure everyone could be there. It was an incredible event for Chrysalis, which is such a great organization. They do such great work, and we were thrilled to help them raise money for a great cause. New Girl fam back together: Jake Johnson, Deschanel, Hannah Simone, Lamorne Morris, Max Greenfield and Damon Wayans Jr. at the Chrysalis Butterfly Ball in Los Angeles on Oct. 10, 2026. Monica Schipper/Getty Images Did you get to hang out or grab a drink afterward? I had to split the night between the event and my sister’s birthday, but I do see everybody fairly often. Since that event, I’ve seen both Lamorne and Hannah — literally last week. I see them all on a regular basis. Looking ahead to 2027, what are you still itching to do? Would you go back to series-regular work? I would, if it were the right project. But I love doing little indie films. I’d love to do more things like Trash Mountain . It was such a great experience, and I love the pace of making independent films. That’s how I started out. Coming from network TV, I like that fast-paced work. It’s very exhilarating. I’d love to do more indie films and stretch my creativity in different ways. When you’re talking with your actor friends, what are the conversations like? The business is in such a strange place, and a lot of people are scared. You have to think creatively and try to work in different ways than you have in the past because the business has changed so much. To me, the one constant in entertainment is that it’s always changing. I feel lucky that I do music as well. When one thing isn’t happening, I’m able to do the other. That’s great for me. But I know there’s been a lot of frustration over the last few years, especially among actor friends, because the nature of being an actor is that you’re often waiting for jobs. Any way you can stretch your creative muscles — whether that’s taking an acting class, getting together with friends, making a film yourself or thinking outside the box — is really helpful. We all do this because we love it at heart. I didn’t get into being an actor for the money. I got into it because I love it. And for some free Bath & Body Works products. Free Bath & Body Works is another plus. Are you a New Year’s resolutions person? Have you identified anything you want to focus on? I’m always making resolutions every day of my life. I’m always thinking, “I’ve got to do more of this.” So I’m not really a New Year’s person, but it is a nice way to reset. I think it’s good to have a north star or something you’re aiming toward. It’s about honing in on what’s important to you and recognizing that you’re happiest when you’re moving toward the things that make you happy. The new year can be a time to think about what makes you happy and how to aim toward those things. See below for more products from the Season of Wonder holiday collection . Candles and a teddy bear holder from Bath & Body Works’ new Season of Wonder holiday collection. “For me, holiday wonder is in the little things you look forward to every year: the scents, the lights and the feeling of finding a gift that is exactly right for someone,” said Deschanel. “The holidays have always been so special to me, and Bath & Body Works is a brand many people associate with the season. I love the quality and care that go into the products, and Season of Wonder is about celebrating all those little things that make the holidays feel special.” Courtesy of Bath & Body Works Vanilla Cocoa Flurries body wash Courtesy of Bath & Body Works Pure Wonder concentrated room spray Courtesy of Bath & Body Works Candles and a teddy bear holder from Bath & Body Works’ new Season of Wonder holiday collection. Writer-director Chris LaMartina has announced “Spirit Tasting,” a spooky New Year’s Eve-themed film from Terror Vision Original Productions. Per the official synopsis, “A post-punk riff on ‘The Monkey’s Paw,’ Chris LaMartina’s ‘Spirit Tasting’ follows three former punks (Sean Doherty, Melissa LaMartina and Trevor Wilhelms) as they toast their late bandmate at a distillery on New Year’s Eve. When a strange sommelier (Matt Lake) invites them to a top-shelf tasting, they discover there’s only one catch: Every bottle requires a ‘wish.’ But as each of their desires twist into doom, these old friends discover that every pour at the Red Bat Distillery comes at a deadly price.” Related Stories Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal The film also stars Matt Baughman, Cate Paris and Tatiana Nya Ford, along with cameos from genre fixtures like Grady Hendrix, Clay McLeod Chapman, Peaches Christ and Henry Zebrowski. Chris LaMartina directed and edited the film, and co-wrote it with Michael Varrati. It is produced by Melissa LaMartina, Chris LaMartina, Varrati and Ted Geoghegan. It’s executive produced by Ryan Graveface. Popular on Variety In the spirit of B-movie icons like Roger Corman, the film was shot in four days for $40,000 in order to celebrate Chris LaMartina’s 40th birthday. The film will also be screening in a holiday roadshow across the country with to-be-announced dates from November to early January. Chris LaMartina and select cast members will appear at each stop. title: The Production Studio, Reimagined
full_text: Oct 26, 2026 9:00am PT Partner Content The Production Studio, Reimagined Traditional production isn’t dead. It’s consolidating around markets that adapt fastest to a net-sum demand through state incentives By Partner Content Plus Icon Partner Content Latest Biggest Names in Media, Entertainment and Sports Will Connect, Collaborate and Make Deals at Jupiter Festival Miami 4 weeks ago How Utopai Studios Is Defining Production Intelligence for Film and Television 4 weeks ago Power at Any Age: Gloria Reuben Urges Menopausal Women to Advocate for Their Health 1 month ago See All The film and television production industry has spent the past several years navigating real headwinds. Productions have followed cost savings overseas, technological innovation has evolved from a talking point to a daily reality on set and in the writers’ room and a widening field of state and international incentive packages has pushed some markets into what looks more like a race to the bottom than a rebound. For studios still operating on the old build-it-and-lease-it model, that shift has been hard to ignore. Related Stories Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal Soundstages aren’t going anywhere. What’s changing is who succeeds with keeping them full, and it’s the operators nimble enough to keep pace with that mantra who inevitably pivot to new ideas. Demand for physical production remains strong in certain key regions of the U.S., but the assumption that four walls and a lease are enough on their own no longer holds. The campuses built to flex with the changes are the ones pulling ahead. Popular on Variety “I still believe in physical production. I believe there will remain a need for boxes that cater to those types of productions,” said Shawn Papazian, president and CEO of The Fields Studios in Chicago. “At the same time, it’s essential to shift flexible design details into a basis and not just building to a pro forma that you think you can financially achieve. Doing something that can work as a campus environment and can host a variety of different creative endeavors is essential.” Papazian frames that shift in practical terms: a facility that can pivot on short notice with soundstages that host a scripted drama one season and an immersive event the next. “This can be everybody’s sandbox,” said RoseMary Prodonovich, general manager of The Fields Studios. “We want to be the epicenter of creative culture in Chicago.” The Balloon Museum, a large-scale art experience from Lux Entertainment, is currently occupying five stages at The Fields Studios. “Managing a production like ours — complex, large-scale and technically demanding with thousands of audiences weekly — requires a strong, reliable partner capable of working in true synergy. With The Fields Studios, we found exactly that,” the company said, pointing to the campus’ “operational flexibility, highly professional team and outstanding stage quality along with their city and state relationships” as central to the partnership. The Fields Studios, a 23-acre mixed-use creative campus on Chicago’s Northwest Side, houses nine soundstages, over 200,000 square feet of production office and support space, on-lot parking, a 1.5-acre backlot, on-site grocery store, retail space and 123 high-end residential lofts, all within the same complex. Built on the site of a century-old manufacturing complex originally constructed in 1928 for Olson Rugs and later home to Marshall Field & Co., it was reimagined, in the words of Papazian, “for producers, by producers.” The connective tissue isn’t just geography; it’s intention. The campus is built to be fluid with a production’s needs — whether film, TV, commercial or immersive activation — rather than forcing every project into the same box. “Producers aren’t just looking for space. They are also looking for comfort,” Papazian said. “They’re looking for a partner who understands the realities of a shooting schedule, a shifting budget and a crew that needs to feel at home.” “Making a show like ‘Dark Matter’ is a huge undertaking and it makes all the difference to have people around you who understand what you’re trying to do,” said Matt Tolmach, executive producer of “Dark Matter” which filmed Season 2 at The Fields Studios last year. “The Fields team gave us a place where our cast and crew could feel at home and focus on making the show. As our needs changed, they were right there with us. They were true partners every step of the way.” Produced by Sony Pictures Television for Apple TV, “Dark Matter” Season 2 is now streaming. That word “home” comes up often at The Fields Studios, and it isn’t incidental. Papazian’s father, Robert A. Papazian, instilled in him a guiding principle when they opened their first studio together more than 30 years ago: productions work long hours, so the space should be cozy and easy to work in. Papazian hand-selected his team from both production and real estate backgrounds, giving the campus an unusual dual fluency. The team understands both what a line producer and their crew need on day one of principal photography and what a real estate owner needs to keep a mixed-use campus financially stable. That legacy extends beyond the property line, too. The Fields Studios team sees the campus’ success as inseparable from the health of Chicago’s broader creative community. They are active with educational institutions and creative organizations across the city, helping to nurture and grow Chicago’s production talent pipeline and foster connections on its world-class campus. That welcoming, production-minded culture, combined with turnkey studio infrastructure and a steadily growing pool of local talent, already makes Chicago an easy choice for productions. Illinois also recently extended and enhanced its production tax credit through 2039, adding higher base incentive rates, expanding eligible expenses and announcing a first-in-the-nation sustainability uplift capable of pushing total savings over 40%. For studios and streamers who have been chasing tax credits and pushing projects away from Los Angeles to Georgia, New York and New Jersey, Illinois is now a top consideration in acquiring that business too. Then there’s the city itself. Chicago’s appeal isn’t confined to what happens inside The Fields Studios’ stages. As Papazian describes the surrounding neighborhoods: “it’s not a backlot, it’s the real thing,” reflecting the city’s genuine architectural range, production history stretching back decades and landscapes that can double for nearly anywhere in the country without a single set built. For productions, that means campus efficiency paired with location diversity, all a short flight from both coasts. “We built this to be a home base, not just a set,” Papazian said. title: ‘Madison’ Horror Game to Get Movie Adaptation From Story Kitchen
full_text: Oct 26, 2026 9:00am PT ‘Madison’ Horror Game to Get Movie Adaptation From Story Kitchen By Todd Spangler Plus Icon Todd Spangler NY Digital Editor xpangler Latest H3 Podcast Crew Cuts Ties With Ethan Klein After Hila Klein Says He Has Been Having an Affair 3 days ago Judge Orders Donald Trump to Testify Under Oath in $10 Billion BBC Defamation Case 4 days ago Trump Says Google CEO Rejected His Request to Rename Atlantic Ocean on Google Maps 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bloodius Games Pulse-pounding psychological horror game “ Madison ” is going to splash some blood on the silver screen. L.A.-based Story Kitchen , a production company specializing in game-to-movie adaptations, has inked a pact with “Madison” developer Bloodious Games to develop a feature film set in the world of the first-person horror title. Currently, there’s no casting info for the “Madison” movie or other details on the production including expected release date, director or screenwriter. The project does not yet have a distribution partner but Story Kitchen is targeting it for a theatrical release. Related Stories Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal In the “Madison” game, you play as Luca Maxwell, who has received an instant camera as a 16th birthday present. Unfortunately for Luca, the camera is inhabited by a demon that forces him to continue a murderous ritual started decades ago by a satanist serial killer (the titular Madison). Players must solve puzzles using the camera to try to break the cycle of madness. Popular on Variety Story Kitchen, co-founded by “Sonic the Hedgehog” movie franchise producer Dmitiri Johnson, is spearheading several other game adaptations. Those include the “Tomb Raider: The Legend of Lara Croft” animated series for Netflix, “Life Is Strange” (Prime Video) and “Streets of Rage” (Lionsgate) . First launched in 2022, “Madison” has received multiple awards and recognitions, including best narrative – grand winner at the NYX Game Awards and best game at EVA 2022. Bloodius also has released an immersive VR version of the game. The partnership with Story Kitchen comes as Bloodious continues to expand the “Madison” universe. The Maxwells’ Curse, a new story expansion, is set to arrive in 2027, free for all “Madison” owners. In addition, a free Halloween update to the game introduces two difficulty modes: an expanded Normal Mode, designed to make the experience more accessible to newcomers to horror and puzzle games; and Possession Mode, an “intense new challenge that pushes even the most experienced players to their limits.” “’Madison’ earned its reputation one heartbeat at a time. Players don’t just remember the story; they remember what it did to them,” Story Kitchen co-founders Dmitri Johnson and Mike Goldberg said. “Our job is to carry that physical experience into a theater without losing what makes it Bloodious’s world.” Bloodious founder Alexis Di Stefano, the game’s creator and director, said, “We built ‘Madison’ to be felt, not just played. Story Kitchen understood from the first conversation that the camera, the house, the Maxwell family, and the terrifying entities behind it all aren’t just set dressing; they’re the franchise. That’s who we wanted to build the next chapter with.” Story Kitchen has a TV first-look deal at Amazon MGM Studios and an animated film first-look deal at DreamWorks Animation. The company is repped by WME and Pryor Cashman. Channing Dungey on Warner Bros. title: Amy Madigan Joins Cast of Paramount+’s ‘Ascent’ With Viola Davis and Sam Heughan
full_text: Oct 26, 2026 9:00am PT Amy Madigan Joins Cast of Paramount+’s ‘Ascent’ With Viola Davis and Sam Heughan By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Executive Editor franklinavenue Latest As His Doc ‘Rather’ Starts Streaming for Free on YouTube, Dan Rather Is More Concerned Than Ever About the Future of Journalism, Especially at CBS News: ‘The Wreckage Is Everywhere’ (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Greg Berlanti to Receive the Paley Center for Media’s Honors Award at Its Fall Gala 4 hours ago Blumhouse Soliciting Testimony from Anyone Who Feels ‘Personally Victimized’ by One of Its Movies or TV Shows 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ian Spanier Oscar winner Amy Madigan (“Weapons”) has joined the cast of Paramount+’s upcoming drama thriller “ Ascent .” She joins previously announced star/exec producer Viola Davis and star Sam Heughan. According to the streamer, Madigan will play “Rachel,” described as “a former executive at Ascent Ventures and Catriona’s (Davis) lifelong mentor.” The casting reunites Madigan with “Ascent” creator John Logan; she previously appeared in Logan’s series “Penny Dreadful: City of Angels.” Related Stories Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal In “Ascent,” which is set in the world of global corporate crisis and damage control, Davis plays “Catriona, an elite corporate fixer, who must weaponize the ruthless skills that have made her indispensable to billion-dollar clients when her estranged daughter is in danger,” while Heughan plays “Conal,” a top Ascent Ventures agent. Popular on Variety Paramount Television Studios is behind the series, which was created by John Logan (“Skyfall,” “Gladiator”). Logan is showrunner and executive producer, while Michael Aguilar (“Penny Dreadful: City of Angels”) and Viola Davis and Julius Tennon for JuVee Productions are also executive producers. Production is set to begin in Los Angeles in 2027. Madigan recently won the best supporting actress Oscar for playing “Aunt Gladys” in “Weapons.” Her other film credits include “Field of Dreams,” “Twice in a Lifetime,” “Gone Baby Gone,” “Uncle Buck,” “Places in the Heart” and “Streets of Fire.” In TV, she won the Golden Globe and was Emmy-nominated for “Roe Vs. title: Robert Pattinson Calls Steven Soderbergh’s ‘The Batman Part II’ Work “Completely Selfless”

Jonathan Olley/Warner Bros./Courtesy Everett Collection Logo text Robert Pattinson is sounding off about Steven Soderbergh stepping up to help finish filming The Batman Part II . Earlier this month, Soderbergh agreed to take the on-set directing reins for the DC Studios production in London after Matt Reeves had to step aside due to a personal family matter back in Los Angeles. Reeves remains involved in the production. “I am so happy he’s come on to help Matt,” Pattinson told Games Radar during a recent interview while promoting the actor’s film Primetime . “It’s incredibly generous of him – and he’s doing it in the loveliest way. So for someone to come in and say, ‘I just want to help Matt do it; I want to do it in conjunction with him and just get it to the edit.’ And to have someone who’s as talented as Steven doing it is great.” Pattinson added the film is now back in production. As previously reported, the plan is for Soderbergh to work in London, while Reeves operates out of Los Angeles. Reeves will also be hands-on during the movie’s post-production in L.A. title: Sofia Franklyn on the Phone Calls That Ended Her Relationship With Alex Cooper
full_text: × Skip to main content Hunter Moreno After months of negotiating with Barstool and Dave Portnoy over the IP for Call Her Daddy , it’s impossible for things not to be tense and charged between me and Alex, and our resentment toward each other for being stuck in this standstill becomes more and more blatant. I feel so worn down. We’re killing ourselves and our friendship by endlessly trying to prove ourselves on diametrically opposed points. I feel severed from the person I’m fighting both against and for. It’s too backward. And mics have been down for weeks. We need to come back alive. Related Stories Business Ethan Klein Says He's Working to "Urgently Remove My Ownership, Financial Stakes" From H3 Podcast After Wife Hila Klein Reveals His Affair Lifestyle 'Clueless' Inspired Kim Kardashian to Buy This Priceless Monet I ask Alex to FaceTime me and remind myself to be nice. I tell her we can stay: “I can’t do this anymore. I just don’t want to roll over on all the points.” She sounds relieved. “No, one hundred percent, totally, yeah. We’re going to make sure we get everything we need.” I get the call from my and Alex’s lawyer Bruce. “Alex is requesting separate representation,” Bruce says. “OK. … Like, you have to represent us as individuals and not as Call Her Daddy ?” “Well, I can still represent you if you want.” “Wait, I’m sorry, I’m so confused. Why would you all of a sudden not represent me? We’ve been doing this for months.” “So, when there’s joint representation and one person decides to seek separate counsel, sometimes people feel it’s … I don’t know, uncomfortable or unfair to use a person they once shared,” Bruce says. “So Alex got her own attorney — she’s not working with us or you anymore?” “That’s correct, but it’s up to you if you want to continue.” I can’t see straight. I feel a pit of fear opening inside me and try to think it away. Maybe separate counsel is smart. We let our lawyers handle it. They can have the tough conversations on our behalf. That’s actually better. We focus on the show, the partnership; we don’t have to live in the intensity anymore. Bruce’s calling again. “Hello?” “Hi, Sofia, one more thing and then I’ll send over that form for you to sign. I reviewed Alex’s contract. Remember you guys told me you had the same agreement, so I was just working off yours, but what was the basis for her higher compensation?” I feel like I’ve been told someone died. “As in, she’s making more money than me?” “Yeah, is that not something you’d talked about?” “No.” “Understood.” I’m silent. “Do you not think that’s weird she lied to you about it?” I press. “Well, it’s something to keep in mind …” Bruce trails off. His unwavering neutrality is off-putting now. His lack of bravado also. But I am putting it in a box for later. I’ll think about it then. I don’t know what else to do. Franklyn (left) and Alex Cooper in 2018. Says Franklyn in the book: “I live in her apartment. Our apartment. I take the train to work with her, then I sit next to her at work, and then I take the train home with her. Together. And then we go to Bubby’s and order pancakes.” Screenshot/YouTube All rationality is gone. The bitch. I feel pure hatred. I might combust. Who is this person? Alex, who is she? Am I stupid? Gullible? Dumb? Naive? Living something that wasn’t true? That’s not true? Was she ever my friend? She was! I saw it. I felt it. I live in her apartment. Our apartment. I take the train to work with her, and then I sit next to her at work, and then I take the train home with her. Together. And then we go to Bubby’s and order pancakes if we feel like it. I’ve seen her cry. She’s seen me. Really seen me. How long has she been carrying this secret? Am I so bad she was scared to tell me? And still is? But this secret is so …small. Who cares? She knows I wouldn’t, if she’d just told me. What was so bad about it that she’d lie to our attorney? Send him into meetings like the village idiot? I think about every contract conversation we’ve ever had. Jokes. How we share every single fucking thing with each other — space, time, emotions, work, pain, highs, shame, heartbreak, family. Alex wouldn’t do this. Lie about something so stupid. To me. When did she start making more money? Why wouldn’t she just tell me about it? Not just as a friend, but while we’re sitting in meetings and calls for six months fighting for fair pay. As CO-OWNERS. Why is she doing this? What is the truth? Muji, Alex’s best friend from high school, the Milfhunter. He’s the only person who can answer my questions, if he’ll even answer my call. We’re on bad terms right now. But are we , really? Alex is the one who fired him. Regardless, if I were him, I wouldn’t want to talk to me either. But who can I talk to? Alex is out of reach now, she’s literally not responding to me, but even if she was, can I trust her at all? Who is this person? I’m confused and angry and disturbed. What is real? Our walks to get pizza, adding red pepper flakes, her skinny wrists bobbing up and down; her legs sprawled out on our new couch, seeing her head cock back in the light of her computer, cackling for hours; doing every single load of laundry together in the 301 basement, half fucking around, half genuinely scared we were going to be murdered; dancing in the living room to Demi Lovato and Kelly Clarkson and Carrie Underwood and Hannah Montana. Was it all fake? Or is dumbass Bruce fake? I’m dropped into a panic attack, all my memories flashing violently in front of me, only to suddenly vanish while I sink into a sea of dread. I try not to drown by repeating things that still feel true, like that calling Muji would be a betrayal to Alex. Our trust is broken, but there must be a reason she lied. There will be an explanation, and I don’t want to commit treason in the process of finding it out. But I can’t live with this mindfuck for another minute without answers. Cooper in 2018. Screenshot/YouTube Muji sends me to voicemail twice, and then picks up. “Whaddup?” Why does he insist on always acting so unbothered? What is this tactic? “Oh, I don’t know, Muji, you used to work at the Barstool office, right? I’m sure you’ve heard a thing or two about what’s been going down.” “No, I haven’t.” Fucker. “I have no one else to talk to about this.” “About what?” “About what? You know exactly what. About ALEX.” “Sorry, but I can’t help you.” “Seriously, Muji?” “I mean, I feel bad, but at the end of the day, I really can’t.” “Did you know about her raise? Like 20K more than me?” I blurt out. Last-ditch effort. “Look, I really wish I could help you …” Click. Barstool Sports, founded by Dave Portnoy (center, in 2023), produced dozens of podcasts — hosted almost entirely by men — but Call Her Daddy was one of the company’s most popular and most lucrative when it ran from 2018 to 2021. Michael Hickey/Getty Images I inhale so hard from my Juul that the pod leaks onto my tongue. Buzz. Buzz. It’s Muji. Back for more. “What’s up?” He sounds chipper now. He might actually be insane. “Cooper doesn’t have friends. I’ve watched it happen since high school, you know what I mean?” I need him to stay on track. “Did you know she was making more money than me?” “I knew the whole time.” “Why wouldn’t she tell me? I wouldn’t even be mad if she had a bonus or something. I’ve said that to her face!!” “She didn’t tell you because she didn’t want you to know she tried to get you fired.” We stay on the phone for another hour, maybe more. I have no sense of reality, much less of the time. Muji tells me Alex has even reached out to him recently, asking him to come on as a producer. Hire him back?? Has she been anticipating a switch-up? He tells me this shit started years ago. I feel like I need to purge the last two years of my life. I want to wash myself from the inside out. All of my memories are violated. Do I need to get my sight checked? What did I miss? It’s not just the last few months. There were secrets even at the peak of our friendship. I thought Muji would give me an answer to today, to our battle with Dave and where to go next. But I know now it goes even further back. Is this who she is? I think about all the times I thought we were sisters, all the moments when it felt like the energy of the world could be generated from us ping-ponging off each other alone. Where did that girl go? Who am I without her? Muji ends the call by repeating that he saw it all coming and hangs up. I’m in shock. No moves left, besides throwing my phone at the wall as hard as I can. title: ‘The Mandalorian and Grogu’ Gets Behind-the-Scenes Book Featuring Original Sketches, Concept Art and Cast Interviews
full_text: If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission. “Star Wars” fans are getting a closer look at how Din Djarin and Grogu made the jump from Disney+ to the big screen. “The Art of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu,” a new 256-page hardcover from Abrams Books, arrives Nov. 3, offering an inside look at the creative process behind Lucasfilm’s latest theatrical release. Written by longtime Lucasfilm collaborator Phil Szostak, the book features previously unseen concept art, early sketches and interviews with the cast. Related Stories Todd Haynes, Zhang Ziyi and Daniel Brühl Lead a Star-Studded Lumière Fest Opening With Haynes Teasing ‘De Noche,’ Starring Pedro Pascal PRE-ORDER NOW In particular, the book explores the visual development of the film’s characters, locations and vehicles. Production design has been a major part of the series since its 2019 debut, combining the Western-inspired aesthetic of the original “Star Wars” films with new environments created using Industrial Light & Magic’s StageCraft technology, which uses LED screens to generate digital backdrops. The book also includes a foreword by Doug Chiang, Lucasfilm’s senior vice president and executive design director, who has worked on the franchise since the prequel trilogy and helped establish the show’s visual style. See two spreads from the book, shared exclusively with Variety , below. Released in May, “ The Mandalorian and Grogu ” marked the franchise’s first theatrical outing since 2019’s “Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker,” bringing one of Disney+’s biggest original properties to cinemas after three seasons on streaming. Created by Jon Favreau, “The Mandalorian” follows the adventures of Pedro Pascal’s helmeted bounty hunter Din Djarin and his Force-sensitive young companion in the years following the fall of the Galactic Empire. Its success spawned a growing collection of interconnected “Star Wars” television projects, including “The Book of Boba Fett” and “Ahsoka,” while helping Disney expand the franchise beyond its traditional theatrical releases. Favreau returned to direct “The Mandalorian and Grogu,” which follows the pair as they take on a new mission for the fledgling New Republic amid lingering threats from Imperial warlords. Pascal reprised his role alongside newcomers Sigourney Weaver and “The Bear” star Jeremy Allen White, who voices Rotta the Hutt, the son of Jabba the Hutt. The upcoming art book continues Abrams’ long-running series of behind-the-scenes “Star Wars” publications, which have become a staple of the franchise’s publishing business. title: How ‘You Can See Everything’ Became a Surprise Box Office Hit (and Likely One of the Biggest Docs of All Time)
full_text: Oct 26, 2026 8:19am PT How ‘You Can See Everything’ Became a Surprise Box Office Hit (and Likely One of the Biggest Docs of All Time) By Rebecca Rubin Plus Icon Rebecca Rubin Senior Film and Media Reporter rebeccaarubin Latest How ‘You Can See Everything’ Became a Surprise Box Office Hit (and Likely One of the Biggest Docs of All Time) 31 minutes ago Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Scores $19.5 Million in Huge Second Weekend, ‘Clayface’ Leads With $24 Million Debut 1 day ago Tom Hanks Returning to Broadway After 14 Years for New Play ‘This World of Tomorrow’ 4 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy Everett Collection “ You Can See Everything ” has remained a must-see at the box office, collecting a remarkable $19.5 million from 2,655 theaters in its second weekend — a notable increase in ticket sales from its sizable opening . A24 ‘s buzzy documentary about Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has grossed $45.1 million domestically to date and will be wildly profitable for the studio against a lean $7 million budget. With electric word-of-mouth, awards chatter and repeat viewings from audiences who are trying to make sense of what they saw on screen, the movie should remain a big-screen draw through the fall. It’s primed to leave theaters as one of the biggest non-musical documentaries of all time, a true feat for a nearly three-hour film that wasn’t publicized until a month before debuting in cinemas. Right now, “Michael Jackson’s This Is It” is the highest-grossing documentary ever with $267 million in 2009, not adjusted for inflation. Meanwhile Michael Moore’s “Fahrenheit 9/11” is the biggest non-music doc with $222 million in 2004, followed by two nature films, “March of the Penguins” with $127 million in 2005 and “Earth” with $107 million in 2007. “You Can See Everything” needs to become a hit overseas to crack the top five. Popular on Variety After a strong second weekend in North America, here are four takeaways from the surprise success of “You Can See Everything.” Restraint bolstered demand A24 began rolling out “You Can See Everything” in 855 theaters, a huge footprint for a documentary. (By comparison, Bleecker Street launched “Musk,” a four-hour look at the world’s richest man, in four locations.) The film opened to $15.6 million — thanks to the more than 2,000 sold-out showings — as cinephiles rushed to theaters to avoid spoilers; the stranger-than-fiction story follows Holmes right before she begins her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors. The decision to launch the movie in moderate release — rather than limited in just a handful of venues or nationwide on more than 2,000 screens — proved wise because the studio was able to bolster awareness while cultivating a sense of scarcity. (In New York City and Los Angeles, good luck catching the film during its first weekend in theaters if you didn’t buy a seat way in advance.) Then ticket sales climbed by 28% as “You Can See Everything” expanded to 2,666 theaters in its second weekend, underscoring the film’s genuine commercial viability beyond the coasts. “Opening ‘You Can See Everything’ in 855 theaters was a really smart move, allowing the film to establish itself and build momentum before going much wider,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “The fact that we’re seeing a documentary deliver such a significant second-weekend increase is remarkable.” Secrecy around the project dialed up the anticipation Nobody knew about the existence of “You Can See Everything” until its surprise world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival in early September. (That’s nothing short of a miracle in Hollywood, where even your waiter knows your P&A spend.) In the scenic Colorado mountain town, the movie became a word-of-mouth sensation after garnering near-euphoric reviews. Shrouding the film in secrecy became an effective marketing tactic. After all, there’s no shortage of movies and television shows about Holmes. Her rise and spectacular fall from grace has been depicted in the Hulu series “The Dropout,” starring Amanda Seyfried, as well as Gibney’s “The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley.” But the immediate sense around “You Can See Everything” was that co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim had captured something very, very different. (And many felt that Holmes had met her match in Fielder, a cringe comedy master best known for HBO’s “The Rehearsal.”) “Bear in mind, the project started with no blueprint or screenplay for how to tell this story,” says analyst David A. Gross, who publishes the box office

title: Anthropic Hopes Potential Investors Do Not Fret About AI’s ‘Catastrophic’ Risks in Its IPO Filing
full_text: Oct 26, 2026 8:19am PT Anthropic Hopes Potential Investors Do Not Fret About AI’s ‘Catastrophic’ Risks in Its IPO Filing By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Anthropic Hopes Potential Investors Do Not Fret About AI’s ‘Catastrophic’ Risks in Its IPO Filing 31 minutes ago Elvis Presley’s Music Owners Sue Anthropic for Copyright Infringement, Demand Nearly $50 Million in Damages 1 hour ago IATSE Names Video Engineer Jillian Arnold First Labor and Technology Officer 3 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images for HubSpot Anthropic spent much of its filing with the SEC ahead of its initial public offering warning potential investors about the risks its AI models could pose to humanity, acknowledging it could not entirely ensure its own safety measures would be successful against the “existential” danger AI could pose. The disclosures came as part of more than 90 pages of risk factors in Anthropic’s S-1 filing with the SEC, made public Monday as the company prepares to go public. The 90-page length of such risk factors, the disclosure of which is customary, is unusual, spurred by the potential dangers AI models have posed following disclosures from AI companies over agents acting autonomously, unaligned with human instructions, and the potential misuse of the technology by human actors themselves. Snap’s risk factors totaled roughly 30 pages, while Elon Musk’s SpaceX — currently the largest IPO of all time at an initial $1.77 trillion valuation — totaled 38. “Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy,” the company wrote, following warnings from a group of current and former Anthropic researchers this summer that the technology posed such risks. Popular on Variety To counter it, Anthropic laid out its sweeping safety-minded policies in its SEC prospectus, a priority for CEO Dario Amodei . Amodei, who founded Anthropic in 2021 with a group of former OpenAI colleagues following their defection from the Sam Altman-founded rival, has advocated for AI companies to band together and slow the development of AI models to ensure sufficient safety protocols. But the company admitted that its own work contributed to such destructive potential: “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.” The company disclosed four separate instances in which its AI models accessed third-party systems without instructions to do so, including one in which an agent changed system settings and read a person’s personal information. The agents all acted independently, without collaborating with other agents, but the company warned that the continued deployment of AI agents risked contributing to more collective — and unauthorized — actions. The company’s risk factors also included factors such as financial commitments, including its billions of dollars worth of compute payments to SpaceX and Microsoft, and technology constraints. Specifically, it warned of Taiwan’s lead in semiconductor manufacturing — and the hostility between Taiwan and China — and the political opposition to data centers as risks to how it performs as a business. But these earthly economic and political factors may not matter much if Anthropic, and the broader AI industry, cannot prevent the models they’re working on from causing cataclysmic doom. “Our safety-focused approach is designed in part to mitigate such risks, but there can be no assurance that our efforts will be successful or that the broader AI industry will adopt similar safeguards,” the company wrote. In the S-1 filing, as is customary, Anthropic did not disclose the number of shares it plans to sell or at what price. Those details will be determined in the coming weeks. The company’s shares will trade under the ticker symbol “ANT” on the Nasdaq exchange. title: ‘Good Girls’ Director on Life in Girls’ Correctional Center in Poland: ‘It Damages You Even More’ (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Oct 26, 2026 8:15am PT ‘Good Girls’ Director on Life in Girls’ Correctional Center in Poland: ‘It Damages You Even More’ (EXCLUSIVE) The film debuts a clip ahead of premiere at Ji.hlava Intl. Documentary Film Festival. Documentary Film Festival Director Ania Winiarska almost gave up on “Good Girls.” “After six months, I felt like I’d hit a wall. I’ve never had this problem before,” she told Variety . “It was always very natural for me to gain people’s trust, but my previous films were about boys or men. This one was about teenage girls and even though I’m a woman, I didn’t realize how much shame they carry. I wasn’t prepared for meeting them.” Related Stories Jessica Biel to Play Hugh Hefner's Wife in 'Playmates' Movie for Searchlight 'Matchbox' Stars Jessica Biel and John Cena Lead New American Red Cross Pledge Drive (EXCLUSIVE) In her doc, premiering at Ji.hlava Intl. Documentary Film Festival, Winiarska enters a Polish correctional center for girls. Some are escaping abuse. Others end up there for skipping school, drinking or dating. Inside, they’re faced with discipline and constant surveillance. Popular on Variety “I was just another adult in a very strict institution where they had to obey all the rules and regulations. I think they viewed me as an outsider, but also as someone who was part of the system,” she recalled. “It took me two years before I could start filming. But once they accepted me, we never had any issues. They would tell all the new girls: ‘She’s good. She’s not a snitch.’” International rights to “Good Girls” are being sold by Stranger Film Sales. Produced by Story, Film i Väst and Tekele Productions, it premieres an exclusive clip here: Winiarska, who is Polish, currently lives in Sweden. She was shocked to discover a world that hadn’t changed for decades. “Most of these people mean well. They try to help the girls, but it’s complicated because this system is so outdated. Rather than trying to catch up with the 21st century, the girls are taught how to cook and sew. Religious classes are no longer compulsory, but they were when I was filming.” Societies may be changing, but the ideas of what constitutes a “good girl” and a “bad girl” are still prevalent. “In some countries, and that includes Poland, good girls are quiet and obedient. Certain prejudices are very much alive,” she noted. “We don’t talk to our children about growing up, puberty or sex education. I was lucky to have parents who cared about me. When I got into trouble, they helped me. If I hadn’t had that, I would probably be one of them.” Most of her young protagonists don’t even fit the center’s profile. “Most of these girls shouldn’t even be there. This place is meant for the resocialization of people who have committed crimes or are on the edge of doing so. But when you look closer, you see they got there because they were skipping school, got pregnant or used drugs or alcohol.” Or simply because they suffer from mental health issues their families cannot or do not want to handle. “One of the girls suffered from depression that wasn’t properly diagnosed. She was lying in bed for three weeks and her mom, who has similar issues, couldn’t help her. Neither did her school. Instead, the police came and handcuffed her in her pyjamas,” said Winiarska. “That’s the problem: they don’t recognize their actual needs. I got quite close to the people who work there, and they also admitted they are not trained as psychologists. When you’re not well mentally and you’re are locked up and punished for it, it damages you even more.” She met girls aged between 10 and 18. “My daughter is 10. It’s scary to think about,” she said. But sometimes the center can provide some safety. “Many of them come from neglectful backgrounds and have experienced all sorts of abuse. At least over there they have regular meals, they go to school, and if they feel bad, there’s someone to talk to. They didn’t have that at home.” There’s another issue, though. Their time at the center restricts their freedom in the present, yet fails to prepare them for the future. “I only started realizing what’s important in life when I was in my 30s. They leave at 18 with a small amount of money. What are they going to do with it? Some party it away or get pregnant over summer breaks. It’s a vicious circle.” Winiarska adds: “These girls are strong. They’re funny. But at that age, you don’t understand the world and the world doesn’t understand you. If, on top of that, you come from a disadvantaged family, it’s easy to sink into a big black hole.” “If this film could change something in our society, it would be so wonderful.” Robert Pattinson Praises Steven Soderbergh for Stepping in to Finish ‘Batman 2′ Filming After Matt Reeves’ Exit: ‘Completely Selfless’ Robert Pattinson Says ‘Batman 2’ Filming Will ‘Pause for a Little Bit’ After Director Matt Reeves Steps Away: ‘We’re Going to Figure It All Out’ ‘The Batman 2’ Pauses Production as Director Matt Reeves Steps Away for a ‘Family Matter’ Robert Pattinson Was Bribed to Star in ‘Primetime’ With 200 Zyn Canisters and a Note That Read: ‘Dear Chris Han-Zyn’ Steven Soderbergh to Help Finish ‘The Batman 2’ Filming After Matt Reeves Stepped Away for Family Matter Sebastian Stan on Why ‘Fjord’ Is Being Called a ‘MAGA Movie’ and How Making ‘The Batman 2’ Feels Like ‘F—ing Godfather Part 2’ Loading comments...

title: Instagram Tests 90-Minute Horizontal Videos In Major Play for Podcasters and Creators
full_text: × Skip to main content By Caitlin Huston Plus Icon Caitlin Huston Business Writer hustonca Follow Sign Up View All October 26, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Instagram's new test of Features, which will play long-form videos on their TV app and phone. Meta Instagram is testing features aimed at capturing a bigger part of the entertainment landscape, including the ability to play long-form videos like podcasts and more on the platform. Starting Monday, Instagram will be launching a test of horizontal videos of up to 90 minutes with select creators in the U.S. The product, called Features, is aimed at podcasters, comedians and other long-form creators, with the ability to refer viewers to the full video from the short-form reels on the platform, which are typically around three minutes or less. “What you’re now going to be able to do is, you see a clip of a podcast that you love, you can just click and continue watching or watch the full video, and you’ll be able to dive in and see the whole thing because creators are going to be able to link these Reels to their overall feature,” said Tessa Lyons, vice president of product at Instagram. Instagram has already been testing the feature with creators in Brazil and has a plan of expanding to tens of thousands of creators in the U.S. The videos will also be recommended to users on Instagram’s Explore page and in other areas. Early creators involved in the test include podcast host and Skims co-founder Emma Grede, beauty and fashion creator Monet McMichael, Preston Rakovsky, who interviews New Yorkers about love and relationships and football content creator Donald De La Haye. This comes as Netflix, Disney and more have been adding podcasts and videos from creators to their platforms, in an effort to capture more consumer viewing hours, and compete with entertainment behemoth YouTube. One challenge for Instagram and others, in the battle against YouTube, has been competing against the platform’s lucrative revenue sharing deals, with YouTube offering qualified creators offered 55 percent of ad revenue and helping generate brand deals. Lyons said Instagram is currently working on “a few different deals” with the early creators for Features, but there’s currently no exclusivity around putting the videos on Instagram (unlike Netflix’s deals for podcasts). Additionally, existing ad deals will carry over into the videos, but Instagram will also work with creators without existing placements to find deals. “For established creators who already have those relationships, they can bring that content with those placements and that branded content. And we also think that there’s a big opportunity for us to help creators who don’t yet have that infrastructure and that business behind them,” Lyons said. Features will be available on mobile, but the goal is to carry the viewing experience over to Instagram for TV, which launched last year with Samsung, Fire TV, Google TV and is now expanding to Apple TV in the U.S. as part of Instagram’s move for more of the entertainment landscape. “We think the best viewing experience for long-form horizontal content is on a big horizontal screen, and so I think that that is where we will expect a lot of the deep consumption to happen over time,” Lyons said. Additionally, given the rise of microdramas, as well as a desire among creators for episodic videos, Instagram has been experimenting with Series, which provides a home for episodic Reels on a creator’s profile. In June, the company began reaching out to microdrama studios in Southeast Asia to experiment with the feature, and has since been reaching out to individual creators, who have been experimenting with their own episodic content. In the coming months, Instagram plans to begin testing the feature in more countries and bring it to the U.S. by the end of year or early next year. The company has also begun testing how it will appear on the TV. These join other new features Instagram has been testing out, including integrating live video into the Reels tab and showing live videos to audience who don’t follow the users. This is launching in Indonesia and Brazil with plans to expand it to the U.S. next year. THR

title: Ava DuVernay Defends Using AI in New Doc ’14th’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All October 26, 2026 8:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Ava DuVernay attends the premiere of '14th' during AFI Fest at TCL Chinese Theatre on Oct. 25. Kevin Winter/Getty Images As Ava DuVernay continues to hit the festival circuit for her new documentary 14th , the director is opening up about her decision to use AI on elements of the film. The doc is a deep dive on the Constitution’s 14th Amendment and the fight over birthright citizenship, featuring archival photographs that are brought to life with the help of AI. This has sparked some criticism online, which DuVernay addressed to The Hollywood Reporter as the doc screened at AFI Fest on Sunday. “The tools that the artists used to do the parallax and the animation in the films have that technology in it, as does Pro Tools with sound, as does Avid with editorial, as does Resolve with color,” she said of industry post-production tools. “I think we’ve come to a place in filmmaking where we have to be really sober about the ways in which that technology is [used] across so much of the workflow.” Related Stories Business Anthropic Warns in IPO Filing That Unfavorable Media Coverage of AI Could "Adversely Affect" Its Business Music Anthropic Sued for Using Elvis Presley Music to Train AI Models She continued of the AI, “We didn’t use it to fabricate a person or make an avatar of a person or approximate someone’s voice that said something they didn’t say. We actually animated some photos that are in the public domain, and from what we’ve been hearing from people it does bring people closer to that time in history, which was our goal. So people have to see it and check it out for themselves and make their decisions about how they feel.” 14th comes a decade after DuVernay’s Oscar-nominated doc 13th , exploring the U.S. prison system and racial inequality in the light of the 13th Amendment. However, she doesn’t see the new film as a direct follow-up, and started considering a return to the Constitution after “hearing the current president talking about his desire to dismantle birthright citizenship while he was a candidate; he said he would do it in his first week in office. He actually did it in his first day in office, he attacked birthright citizenship.” “I don’t know much about the 14th Amendment at that point but I know birthright citizenship is in it. So we start thinking about the possibility of making this film at that point,” the filmmaker said, and “once we saw all of the tentacles of the current administration attacking this amendment, we knew that there was more there. So we investigated it and that’s what the film became.” 14th will get a limited theatrical run starting Nov. 27, and start streaming on Netflix on Dec. 4. THR

title: Anthropic Warns in IPO Filing That Unfavorable Media Coverage of AI Could “Adversely Affect” Its Business
full_text: × Skip to main content By Alex Weprin Plus Icon Alex Weprin Senior Editor alexweprin Follow Sign Up View All October 26, 2026 7:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Dario Amodei Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images Anthropic, one of the two biggest artificial intelligence labs (alongside OpenAI) filed to go public Monday morning, and alongside platitudes about the wondrous potential of the technology (curing disease that has vexed humanity for centuries!) and the terrifying downside possibilities (“catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”), it warned of the looming threat of the media to its ongoing business. The company, founded by Dario Amodei, is one of the leading frontier labs developing AI tech, but as the company noted in its S-1 filing with the SEC Monday, the public perception of it may pose a serious threat to its ability to continue operating. The filing also noted the risks posed by copyright law, as well as the company’s priorities, including a section that calls out a divergence from OpenAI that may be relevant to Hollywood. But it is the threats of negative media coverage that comes up again and again in the filing, with the risk factors section spelling it out most clearly: “As our business has grown and as interest in us and the AI industry overall has increased, we have attracted, and may continue to attract, significant media coverage, public commentary, and scrutiny from time to time. This coverage and commentary have included, and we expect will continue to include, recurring narratives concerning the potential adverse societal impacts of AI, including that AI may displace or eliminate jobs, may be misused or otherwise cause harm, and may pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” the filing states. “Negative media coverage, including public figures making negative or threatening statements about our company, whether accurate or not, could also adversely affect our brand and reputation and may reduce market acceptance of our models, platform, and applications or impair our ability to attract and retain customers,” it adds. “As public awareness of our brand increases, any issues that draw media attention may have an amplified adverse effect on our reputation. If unfavorable media coverage or adverse public perceptions persist or intensify, the demand for our models, platform, and applications could decline and our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.” As for Hollywood, the litigation threat around copyrighted works remains top of mind for the company, which listed all of the lawsuits and threat letters related to books, films, music and other copyright holders, with the company noting that it may require them to acquire a license to the material, which they may or may not be able to secure. The legal landscape around AI and IP remains deeply uncertain. “In each of the actions, we believe we have meritorious defenses and dispute any allegation of wrongdoing,” the company wrote. “Legal proceedings related to these matters can have an adverse effect on us because of defense and settlement costs individually and in the aggregate, diversion of management resources, and other factors.” And then there’s the video element. There are a swarm of startups looking to use the technology to transform entertainment, but Anthropic, unlike SpaceX and OpenAI, has never spent resources on video or image models. The company notes as much in its filing: “Every research project must ultimately advance our mission. This focus also guides what we choose not to pursue,” it says. “For example, we do not currently focus on developing video and image generation models, despite their commercial appeal. That compute instead goes to coding, agentic skills, and safety research—a research decision that has also aided the capital efficiency of our models.” Also unlike OpenAI or SpaceX, Anthropic does not have an advertising business, and while it does spend some on ads (like at the Super Bowl) it is hardly a major player. The company disclosed $147 million in advertising spend in 2025, with marketing and advertising expenses rising by $273 million in the first half of this year “reflecting higher media spend to support product launches.” THR

title: Doha Film Festival Unveils 2026 Jury Headed By Naomi Kawase
full_text: Skip to main content By Melanie Goodfellow Melanie Goodfellow Senior International Film Correspondent @mel_goodfellow More Stories By Melanie Edinburgh Film Festival Genre Title ‘Snapshot’ Gets North American Deal Charades Boards Juho Kuosmanen’s ‘Dream Come True’ As Production Wraps Across Europe Watermelon Pictures Acquires North American Distribution Rights To Sara Ishaq’s ‘The Station’ View All October 26, 2026 5:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source L-R: Gianfranco Rosi, Adam Bessa, Centre: Naomi Kawase L-R: Dora Bouchoucha, Kamal Aljafari L-R: Courtesy, Centre: Leslie Kee, L-R: Rim Temimi, Ferrante Ferranti Japanese director Naomi Kawase has been unveiled as the head of the jury for the main international competition of the upcoming second edition of the Doha Film Festival in November. She will be joined by French Tunisian actor Adam Bessa , Tunisian producer Dora Bouchoucha, Italian documentary filmmaker Gianfranco Rosi and award-winning Palestinian filmmaker and artist Kamal Aljafari. The jury will decide the winning films from the 15-film line-up of international titles, from across the Arab world, Asia, Africa, Europe and the Americas. Related Stories News 'Paper Tiger' & Furies' Set For Doha Film Festival Gala Screenings News Doha Film Festival To Showcase Four Qatari Features In Milestone Moment For Local Industry Born and based in Nara, Japan, Cannes regular Kawase became the youngest recipient of its Caméra d’Or for her debut feature, Suzaku , before winning the Grand Prix for The Mourning Forest (2007). Her film Radiance (2017) received the Ecumenical Jury Prize at Cannes, while her latest feature, Yakushima’s Illusion (2025), premiered in competition at Locarno. Watch on Deadline She has previously been a guest of the Doha Film Institute , which is overseeing the festival, as one of the so-called Masters in 2016 of the body’s annual Qumra event, mentoring emerging filmmakers from Qatar and beyond. Acto r Bessa broke out internationally in Lotfy Nathan’s Harka (2022), which earned him the Best Performance Award in the Un Certain Regard section at Cannes and Best Actor at the Red Sea International Film Festival. He subsequently starred in Meryam Joobeur’s Who Do I Belong To (2024), which competed at the Berlinale, and Jonathan Millet’s Ghost Trail , earning further acclaim and a César nomination. In 2026, he appeared in Asghar Farhadi’s Parallel Tales . DFI supported all three of his films, Harka , Who Do I Belong To and Parallel Tales . Bouchoucha is one of the Arab world’s most influential film producers and a longstanding advocate for emerging filmmakers. Working under the banner of her 30-year-old company Nomadis Images in 1995, her credits include Satin Rouge , Inhebbek Hedi , Weldi , Behind the Mountains , Souad and Aisha Can’t Fly Away . Rosi is the only documentary filmmaker to have won both the Golden Lion at Venice and the Golden Bear at Berlin. His film Sacro GRA (2013) became the first documentary to win Venice’s Golden Lion, while Fire at Sea (2016), filmed on the island of Lampedusa, won the Golden Bear and the European Film Award and received an Academy Award nomination. His documentary Notturno (2020) was presented in competition at Venice, and Below the Clouds (2025) won the festival’s Special Jury Prize. He was a also DFI Qumra Master in 2018. Aljafari is recognized for his distinctive cinematic practice exploring memory, history, identity and the politics of images. His feature A Fidai Film (2024) won the Jury Prize in the Burning Lights Competition at Visions du Réel and the Tanit d’Or at Carthage. His documentary With Hasan in Gaza (2025) received Best Artistic Achievement at Doha Film Festival. Both films were supported by DFI, which is also backing his forthcoming feature Beirut 1931 . “Independent cinema is where the most vital, courageous and transformative stories of our time find their voice. It is our responsibility to protect the creative freedom to challenge conventions, bring overlooked perspectives to the screen and build bridges across cultures,” said Fatma Hassan Alremaihi, CEO of Doha Film Institute and Director of Doha Film Festival . “We are immensely proud to welcome friends of the Institute who share our vision and have dedicated their lives to nurturing independent cinema. Their collective experience and artistic integrity embody the spirit of DFI and DFF: championing original voices, creating space for bold ideas and ensuring that powerful stories, find their way to audiences around the world.” The Doha Film Festival, which expands on the DFI’s long-running family-focused festival of Ajyal which ran for more than a decade during the same period, will unfold from November 19 to 27. ‘Clayface’ Takes No. 1 With $24M, But ‘See Everything’ Draws Nearly $20M Donald Trump Posts 1,300-Word Diatribe Against Bill Maher After Their Dinner Saif Ali Khan, Vidya Balan & Mélanie Laurent Set For Ritesh Batra Pic Russell Brand’s Former Assistant Alleges “Insane Sexual Appetite” Read More About: Comments
